summary:
Djibouti's penal code contains no express offence criminalising consensual same-sex conduct. Sections 353 and 354 refer vaguely to "good morals" and public morality without naming same-sex relations, and no provision states the position either way. Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, nevertheless marks same-sex relations as not lawful throughout the country in its at-a-glance assessment, and authorities retain the power to prosecute public same-sex conduct under these articles. The practical position is that such conduct is treated as de facto illegal despite the absence of an express offence.

Public-morality and "obscene acts" provisions are used against people. No reported case law defines the outer limits of Sections 353 and 354, so the exposure of a trans visitor who is visible, or who engages in any conduct in a public setting that would be read as sexual or obscene, is undefined by statute and depends on how authorities apply the provisions.

Djibouti provides no legal gender recognition, and LGBTI organisations cannot register. Wikipedia's overview records that discrimination protection exists in employment only, while the US State Department's 2023 human rights report states there is no legal prohibition of discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. The two sources differ on the scope of any employment protection.

Social and religious intolerance is pervasive. The 2023 State Department report describes status and conduct as taboo, with a societal pattern of discrimination and no official violence cases that can be cited. People fear family and community shunning on disclosure. Wikipedia records that no public societal discussion of homosexuality is tolerated.

Complaints about discrimination can be filed with the police or with the national human-rights commission (CNDH). The 2023 State Department report cites no official violence cases, so the practical reach of that route is not documented.
tangentialFactors: The legal position is ambiguous rather than settled: no statute names same-sex conduct, no case law interprets the "good morals" provisions, and the sources disagree on whether any employment discrimination protection exists. A visitor's exposure therefore rests on enforcement practice rather than on a defined offence.
localsOnly: Djibouti provides no legal gender recognition, and LGBTI organisations cannot register as associations. Residents who wish to complain of discrimination can approach the police or the national human-rights commission (CNDH). The 2023 State Department report records no legal prohibition of discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, while Wikipedia records protection in employment only.
outOfScopeNotes:
No reported case law defines the outer limits of Sections 353 and 354, and the 2023 State Department report cites no official violence cases, so the enforcement record is not documented.

The US State Department's 2015 human rights report for Djibouti carried limited LGBT-specific content; the remainder addressed general conditions including suppression of the opposition, prison conditions, female genital mutilation and trafficking.

A Canadian Immigration and Refugee Board response to information request covering research from 2009 to March 2012 found documentation on the treatment of sexual minorities in Djibouti scarce across all consulted sources, relying on the US 2010 country report. It is a dated baseline for the legal and protection framework and support services of that period, not a current assessment.
